\subsection{Direction Asymmetry and Quality Confounding}
\label{sec:direction}

The formality axis exhibits a pronounced direction asymmetry: the judge selects the formal variant in 78.8\% of formal-is-rewrite pairs ($p = 0.001$) but only 54.5\% of casual-is-rewrite pairs ($p = 0.83$).
This asymmetry suggests that original quality $Q$ and formality $S$ are partially confounded---formally written texts may be inherently perceived as higher quality.
To quantify this, we fit a logistic decomposition (GEE, exchangeable correlation) with both formality and original-preference as predictors.
After controlling for original preference, the formality effect remains significant ($\text{OR} = 2.21$, 95\% CI $[1.21, 4.04]$, $p = 0.010$), while the original-preference effect is marginal ($\text{OR} = 1.82$, 95\% CI $[1.00, 3.32]$, $p = 0.052$).
The formality preference thus survives adjustment for original-preference confounding, though the marginal original-preference effect indicates that this confound is non-negligible.

Table~\ref{tab:gee} compares the GEE decomposition across judges and axes.
The Qwen3-32B formality effect ($\text{OR} = 4.20$, $p = 0.0002$) is roughly twice the GPT-4o estimate ($\text{OR} = 2.21$, $p = 0.010$), and the originality confound is substantially stronger ($\text{OR} = 4.70$ vs.\ $1.82$).
This amplification is consistent with evaluator-producer bias (\S\ref{sec:limitations}): because Qwen3-32B generated the rewrites, it may partially recognize its own outputs, inflating both the style and originality effects.
The directional agreement between judges---both favor formal text after controlling for originality---supports the existence of formality bias, but the effect magnitude from Qwen3-32B should not be directly compared with GPT-4o.

The ordinal logistic regression (ordered model, logit link, $n = 88$ pairs, 176 observations) correctly respects the ordinal nature of Likert data without assuming equal intervals between scale points.
Without pair random effects, the ordered model treats observations as independent, which is anti-conservative (favors detecting an effect).
Despite this favorable statistical bias, the formality coefficient remains non-significant ($\beta = -0.079$, 95\% CI $[-0.60, 0.45]$, $p = 0.769$), and GEE with pair-level clustering confirms ($p = 0.587$).
This rules out the possibility that the Blindspot is an artifact of inappropriate interval-scale ATE analysis---the limitation is inherent to Likert measurement itself.

The key finding is the magnitude gap between measurement methods: Likert scores are indistinguishable from chance regardless of statistical approach ($p \geq 0.33$), while pairwise comparison detects a clear preference ($p = 0.006$).

\paragraph{Threshold sensitivity.}
\label{sec:nli_threshold}
The 0.90 NLI threshold is not a cliff edge.
The formality win rate is stable at 72.3--73.9\% across thresholds of 0.70, 0.90, and 0.95 (sign test $p < 0.005$ at every threshold).
NLI scores follow a bimodal distribution: the majority of pairs score above 0.95 or below 0.30, with few observations in the 0.80--0.95 range.
The 0.90 threshold is consistent with standard DeBERTa-v3-large NLI calibration and lies on a plateau of the score distribution, not a cliff edge.
This bimodality reflects the binary nature of the rewriting task: rewrites either preserve content well (high NLI) or introduce semantic drift (low NLI), with little middle ground.
